new_statements.quote: 2.2.4 Stress. Stress placement is not predictable and is in fact phonemic as is shown by the minimal pair [ˈařaǰa] 'wave' - [ařˈaǰa] 'salty'. Examples of variation in stress placement are [kˈɑǰo] 'grub', [au̯ˈi] 'heron', [met̪akˈɔ] 'wing', [it̪ˈane] 'sun', [ˈuřaŋge] 'rain'. [p. 19:] Judging by the Weriagar data Anceaux was right regarding the absence of tense markers in the verb, the freedom of accent placement, and the behaviour of word-final vowels. But in Weriagar it is the stressed vowel which is lengthened and stress is not always marked by a high pitch.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Kemberano (Weriagar dialect) is free and lexically fixed: its position is not predictable from the shape of the word and is contrastive (minimal pair 'wave' vs 'salty'); the cited examples show stress on the initial, a medial, or the final syllable. The stressed vowel is lengthened; high pitch is a common but not obligatory correlate. For the Barau dialect Anceaux (quoted p. 19) likewise found no simple placement rule, with the accent realised as high pitch.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Anceaux (quoted p. 19) notes for Barau that unaccented final vowels tend to become nearly inaudible or disappear, which Voorhoeve confirms for Weriagar (p. 6 reports final-vowel devoicing).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from elicited citation forms and short phrases; survey data from a single Weriagar speaker (about six hours, recorded in Manokwari, Aug-Sep 1982). The statement is made in the Weriagar section (sec. 2, the main body of the sketch). No phrase-level or intonation discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Voorhoeve 1985 describes 'Arandai', which Glottolog splits into Kemberano kemb1235 [bzp] (his Weriagar dialect = weri1246, villages Weriagar, Taroi, Kalitami; his Barau dialect = bara1347, Tomage/Otaweri on the Bomberai) and Dombano aran1237 [jbj] (his Sebyar dialect, villages Tomu, Arandai, Kecap); his Tarof and Kasuweri are now assigned to Kokoda. The explicit stress statement (sec. 2.2.4, p. 7) belongs to the Weriagar dialect, i.e. Kemberano proper, and the p. 19 accent remark (via Anceaux 1958) to Barau, also Kemberano. The same page was used by the aran1237 check for Dombano by extension ('phonetically very similar', p. 17); for kemb1235 it is first-hand. Berry & Berry 1987: 94 and de Vries 2024: 237 confirm Kemberano = Kalitami/Weriagar = Barau.
